extracted.intended_audience: copyright applicants, creators, registrants, policymakers, and copyright/legal practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Assessment of the legal standards and practical guidance for when outputs generated with or incorporating AI are eligible for U.S. copyright protection, and how to approach registration. Includes analysis of human contribution, originality, prompts, expressive inputs, and policy considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human authorship requirement (bedrock)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protection in the United States requires human authorship; 'human authorship is a bedrock requirement of copyright.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is grounded in the Copyright Clause and court decisions (e.g., Thaler). No court has recognized copyright in material created by non-humans. Registration practice and litigation interpret the statute to require an identifiable human author. Example: court affirmed refusal to register a work described as 'autonomously created by a computer algorithm.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality standard (minimal creativity required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects original expression; originality requires a creative spark but the threshold is low ('even a slight amount will suffice'). Sweat-of-the-brow (mere effort) is not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Feist: assess whether the human contribution contains more than mere facts/ideas or mechanical effort. Even modest creative choices can meet originality. Use case-specific analysis of the creative spark present in the human contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea/expression dichotomy and non-protectability of facts/ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas, facts, and suggestions are not protectable; only the author's expression is copyrightable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between providing an idea or direction (unprotectable) and contributing an expression fixed in a tangible medium. Cases (e.g., CCNV, Andrien) show that detailed instructions or commissioning alone may be insufficient to create authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assistive (tool) use of AI does not defeat copyrightability
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of AI tools to assist rather than stand in for human creativity does not affect the availability of copyright protection for the output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If AI functions as an assisting instrument and the resulting expressive elements are human-authored or reflect human creative choices, the work (or the human contribution) can be protected. Example: the Office registered a sound recording created using a special-purpose AI vocal model developed under the human artist’s supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely AI-generated material is not copyrightable
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright does not extend to purely AI-generated material, or material where there is insufficient human control over the expressive elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a work is 'entirely generated by AI' with no human role in determining expressive elements, courts and the Office have rejected copyright protection (e.g., Thaler decision rejecting registration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of human contribution analyzed case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether human contributions to AI-generated outputs are sufficient to constitute authorship must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No bright-line rules; examine the nature, degree, and quality of human creative input. Consider which expressive elements are perceptibly human-authored, and whether human choices shaped those elements sufficiently to meet authorship/originality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompts alone are unlikely to provide sufficient control
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the functioning of current generally available technology, prompts do not alone provide sufficient control to establish authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although prompts can be detailed and 'prompt engineering' exists, AI outputs remain unpredictable ('black box' behavior, non-deterministic outputs, variable reproducibility even with seeds). Thus, prompting by itself typically will not satisfy the human authorship requirement absent additional human expressive contribution or control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-authored expressive inputs included in outputs are protectable
rubrics_metrics.description: Human-authored expressive inputs (text, images, audio, etc.) that are incorporated into AI-generated outputs can be protected as human-authored expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the human-created input is perceptible in the AI output, the human retains copyright in that expressive material. Registration may cover those human-authored elements even if other portions of the output are AI-generated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative selection, coordination, arrangement, and modifications are protectable
rubrics_metrics.description: Human creative selection, coordination, or arrangement of material in AI outputs, and creative modifications of AI-generated outputs, can constitute protectable authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office has registered works where the human-authored selection/arrangement of AI material or creative modifications were the basis for protection (e.g., registrations covering human-authored text and the human-authored selection, coordination, and arrangement of elements). Courts (Burrow-Giles, CCNV) recognize that these human contributions can supply the necessary authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptibility of human contribution in final output
rubrics_metrics.description: Human authors are entitled to copyright in their 'works of authorship that are perceptible in AI-generated outputs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on whether the human-contributed expression can be perceived in the end product. If perceptible, those expressive elements are eligible for protection even if surrounded by AI-generated material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure requirement for registration when AI material exceeds de minimis
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work contains more than a de minimis amount of AI-generated material, the applicant should disclose that information and provide a brief statement describing the human author’s contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the Office’s AI Registration Guidance: applicants should identify AI-generated content beyond de minimis and explain the nature of human contributions. The Office will register the human author’s contribution and may refuse registration for non-human material.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI cannot be a joint author; joint authorship requires a copyrightable contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI system cannot be a co-author; to be a joint author a human must make a copyrightable contribution (not merely supply ideas or instructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use joint-authorship analogies: a person must 'translate an idea into an expression' or make creative contributions embodied in the work. Merely specifying or directing the output (without contributing protectable expression) does not create joint authorship with the system or make the user an author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpredictability and opacity of AI models affect authorship/control
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'black box' nature, non-determinism, and unpredictability of many generative AI models may limit a user’s ability to show sufficient human control over expressive elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider technical limits: model scale, stochastic outputs, seed/reproducibility limitations, and internal complexity. These factors weigh against finding that a human has controlled or authored the expressive content when outputs cannot be reliably attributed to a user's directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No present case for additional copyright or sui generis protection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office concluded that 'the case has not been made for additional copyright or sui generis protection for AI-generated content.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy recommendation: existing doctrines are adequate for now; continue monitoring developments. The Office does not recommend creating a separate form of protection at this time absent future developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy considerations for legal change (incentives, access, competition, clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments for and against extending protection to AI-generated works include (A) providing incentives to create, (B) empowering creators with disabilities (where AI is a tool), (C) countering international competition, and (D) providing greater clarity for creators and markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are evaluative policy factors the Office considered in assessing whether legislative change is desirable. They are not legal thresholds but inform whether reform should be pursued. The Office weighed competing concerns (e.g., creator incentives vs. proliferation of AI outputs) and emphasized constitutional and doctrinal constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration practice and practical consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office will register human-authored contributions in works that incorporate AI-generated material and continues to update guidance and the Compendium to assist the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registration provides practical benefits (e.g., presumption of validity, ability to sue). Applicants should follow registration guidance (disclosure and description of human contribution). The Office will monitor developments and may revise practices as needed.
